A line complication occurred in 14.6 percent of courses: occlusion in 6.1 percent, upper-limb venous thrombosis in 3.0 percent, line-associated bloodstream infection in 1.2 percent and dislodgement in 4.3 percent. Complications were more frequent with vancomycin infusions, double-lumen lines and courses longer than four weeks, and most occurred in the first three weeks. Data came from hospital records only, so events managed by community nurses without a hospital visit were not captured. The authors call for community data in future studies."},{"title":"Midline catheters versus peripherally inserted central catheters for outpatient intravenous antibiotics: a propensity-matched comparison","authors":"Vasquez-Lindahl R, Osei-Brandt K","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Outpatient Antimicrobial Care","doi":"10.5555/joac.2022.0310","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 1,340 outpatient antibiotic courses, 512 midline courses were matched to 512 courses using peripherally inserted central catheters on antibiotic, planned duration and kidney function. Midlines had fewer line-associated bloodstream infections (0.4 versus 1.4 percent) but more premature removals for occlusion or dislodgement (11.9 versus 7.2 percent). For courses planned to last more than 14 days, the difference in infections was smaller and premature removal was twice as common with midlines. Vesicant antibiotics were excluded from midline use by local policy. Residual confounding by the clinician's choice of line is likely."},{"title":"Living with a line: patients' and carers' experiences of home intravenous antibiotic therapy","authors":"Thornbury-Mensah A, Laurent-Okoye F","year":2021,"venue":"Home Infusion Practice Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke at length with 22 patients and 9 family carers receiving intravenous antibiotics at home through a long line. Participants described the line as both a lifeline and a constant worry. Many were unsure how to protect the dressing when washing, and some avoided using the arm altogether. Several patients delayed reporting swelling or a sluggish line because they did not want to seem difficult or feared readmission. Carers who flushed lines themselves wanted hands-on teaching rather than a leaflet. Conversations took place at one service and participants were chosen by the nursing team, which may have excluded the most dissatisfied."},{"title":"Variation in flushing and dressing practice between home infusion nursing teams and its association with catheter occlusion","authors":"Hallberg-Nwachukwu E, Pereira-Dunmore S, Ito-Castellano J","year":2016,"venue":"Home Infusion Practice Review","doi":"10.5555/cin.2016.0056","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across four home infusion nursing teams serving 610 outpatient antibiotic courses, we recorded the flushing method, locking solution and dressing change interval at each visit. Occlusion rates ranged from 3.1 percent to 11.8 percent between teams. Teams using a pulsatile flushing technique had fewer occlusions after adjustment for line type and antibiotic. Dressing changes were late in 18 percent of visits, and late changes were more common at weekends. Documentation of flushing was missing from 23 percent of visit notes, which limited the analysis and may have hidden differences between individual nurses."},{"title":"Vascular access complications in outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Rahman-Oduya S, Lindqvist-Barros H, Nakashima-Ellis C, Ferreira-Kamau D","year":2023,"venue":"Outpatient Infection Therapy Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/ida.2023.0412","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 38 observational studies of adults receiving outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy. The pooled incidence of any line complication was 9.8 per 1,000 catheter days, with wide variation between studies. Thrombosis was reported more often in studies that screened with ultrasound. Only six studies reported complications managed in the community, and none measured patient-reported outcomes. Definitions of occlusion and dislodgement differed across studies, most studies were single-centre and retrospective, and small studies reporting low complication rates were under-represented, suggesting reporting bias."},{"title":"Line care teaching for patients discharged on home intravenous therapy: a regional service evaluation","authors":"Regional Infection Services Network","year":null,"venue":"Regional infection services evaluation series","providerType":"report","abstract":"A regional network evaluated the teaching given to patients discharged with a long line for home intravenous therapy. Of 140 patients asked at their first community visit, 61 could describe how to keep the dressing dry and 48 knew which symptoms to report the same day. Patients taught with a demonstration and a return demonstration answered more questions correctly than those given a leaflet alone. The report does not state when the data were collected, gives no detail of how patients were selected, and contains no information on line complications or unplanned hospital visits."},{"title":"Home infusion nurses' views on line problems during outpatient antibiotic therapy: a focus group study","authors":"Achebe-Lorimer N, Sorensen-Iwu P","year":2024,"venue":"Home Infusion Practice Review","doi":"10.5555/cin.2024.0091","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held six focus groups with 31 nurses from two home infusion agencies. Nurses described line problems as often starting between visits and being noticed late. They reported unclear responsibility for escalating a sluggish line, difficulty reaching the hospital team out of hours, and inconsistent orders for flushing and locking. Nurses felt that hospital records rarely showed the problems they solved at home, such as replacing a lifted dressing or restoring flow. They asked for a shared escalation pathway and one set of line care orders agreed between the hospital and the agencies."},{"title":"Explaining variation in unplanned hospital returns during outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy: an explanatory sequential study","authors":"Mwangi-Holloway D, Castellanos-Reiter B, Oduya-Pham L","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Outpatient Antimicrobial Care","doi":"10.5555/joac.2025.0044","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We first analysed 902 outpatient antibiotic courses and found that line problems caused 38 percent of unplanned returns to hospital, concentrated in patients living alone and in courses managed by one of two agencies. We then spoke with 17 patients and 12 nurses selected from the extremes of the quantitative results. The conversations explained the agency difference by differences in weekend staffing and in how nurses escalated sluggish lines. Patients living alone described difficulty noticing arm swelling and reaching help. Integrating both strands changed the service's priority from line choice to escalation and teaching."}]}
